title: Slow-Moving Nor'easter Floods the Northeast, Cutting Power to 100,000
summary:
A powerful, slow-moving storm is creeping along the northeast U.S. coast this weekend, and it's causing serious problems. The nor'easter — a storm that travels up the Atlantic coast — has knocked out electricity to about 100,000 customers, whipped up huge waves, and dumped heavy rain across the mid-Atlantic and New England. Tens of millions of people are in its path, and forecasters say there's no quick end in sight.

"There will be a lot of high winds, a lot of high tides and heavy rain possibility over the next few days for the northeastern U.S.," said Bob Oravec, lead forecaster with the National Weather Service in College Park, Maryland.

At Surf City Marina on the Jersey Shore, owner Kenny Formica sat at home watching surveillance cameras as water rose inside his building. That's rare — the last time he remembers it happening was during Hurricane Sandy, which caused more than $4 million in damage to his business. Before the storm, workers secured dock lines, moved equipment, and parked trucks and forklifts on the highest ground. By Saturday morning, even those were nearly surrounded by water. "This is like an 8,000-pound boat and, you know, a $150,000 boat — just gone," Formica said.

In Edgewater, New Jersey, water spilled into a parking lot packed with cars. Video on social media showed one car almost completely submerged, with only its sunroof above the water.

The storm scrambled travel and sports plans too. Hundreds of flights were cancelled at Boston Logan International Airport, along with most flights to Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket. The Boston Red Sox and Chicago Cubs, preparing for the playoffs, played a double-header Friday and moved their Sunday finale to Florida. Singer Ed Sheeran cancelled two concerts at Gillette Stadium.

In North Carolina, a highway closure on Hatteras Island stranded most of the roughly 45 guests invited to Jayden Sink and Kimberly Laprad's wedding. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said coastal flooding is the biggest threat, with waves up to six metres. "The rain is underway," she warned, "and mark my words: Much more is coming."
why_it_matters: A slow storm like this shows how fast normal life can stop — school, sports, travel and power — and how much coastal communities have to prepare for the extreme weather that will shape the future today's students grow up in.

background_read: Nor'easters are a regular danger on the U.S. East Coast, especially in fall and winter: they form when cold northern air crashes into warm ocean air, and because they move so slowly they can pound the same beaches for days.
Hurricane Sandy (a huge 2012 storm that flooded New York and New Jersey and caused billions of dollars in damage) is the storm many coastal residents still measure other storms against.
The National Weather Service (the U.S. government agency that issues weather forecasts and warnings) is the body whose forecasters, like Bob Oravec, warn the public.

Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket (two islands off the coast of Massachusetts, popular summer destinations) lose most of their flights in big storms because they depend heavily on small planes and ferries.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (New York's governor since 2021) warned that coastal flooding, not wind, is the biggest threat, with waves up to six metres.

perspectives.description: They see early, detailed warnings as a success: people had time to move boats, park equipment on high ground and change travel plans before the worst arrived, which saves lives and money.
For people like Kenny Formica, every big storm is a gamble on whether they can keep rebuilding in a flood-prone spot — and whether insurance will ever cover the losses.
Nor'easters are a normal feature of the East Coast's weather, not a freak event. What makes them destructive is their slow speed: the same coastline gets hit again and again for days instead of once.

perspectives.perspective: Local officials and residents looking ahead
perspectives.description: The storm raises questions about stronger sea walls, better drainage, buried power lines and clearer evacuation plans — tough, expensive choices for towns that flood more often than they used to.
